items.stem: Define the term "ATP".
items.answer: Adenosine triphosphate, a nucleotide that acts as the immediately available energy currency of the cell
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: adenosine triphosphate, a nucleotide that acts as the immediately available energy currency of the cell. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Why is ATP a suitable energy currency?
options: It releases energy in small, usable amounts when hydrolysed and is easily regenerated.
items.answer: It releases energy in small, usable amounts when hydrolysed and is easily regenerated.
items.markingKey: D. Immediate energy.

items.stem: Why does anaerobic respiration produce far less ATP than aerobic respiration?
options: Glucose is only partly broken down and there is no oxidative phosphorylation.
items.answer: Glucose is only partly broken down and there is no oxidative phosphorylation.
items.markingKey: A. Only glycolysis yields ATP.

items.stem: A respirometer containing soda lime and 6.7 g of blowfly larvae was used. The coloured liquid moved 72 mm in 5 minutes along a capillary of radius 0.75 mm. Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake in mm³ g⁻¹ min⁻¹.
items.answer: 3.80 mm³ g⁻¹ min⁻¹
items.markingKey: V = πr²d = π × 0.75² × 72 = 127 mm³ (M1); ÷ 5 min ÷ 6.7 g = 3.80 mm³ g⁻¹ min⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem:
Pondweed (Elodea) was placed in 1 % sodium hydrogencarbonate solution at 25 °C. A lamp was placed at different distances and the number of bubbles released per minute was counted.

Distance / cm | Relative light intensity (1/d² × 10⁴) | Bubbles per minute
10 | 100.0 | 33
15 | 44.4 | 23
20 | 25.0 | 16
30 | 11.1 | 8
40 | ? | 5
50 | 4.0 | 3

(a) Calculate the relative light intensity at 40 cm. [1]
(b) Calculate the percentage increase in bubble rate from 50 cm to 10 cm. [2]
(c) Describe the relationship between light intensity and the rate of photosynthesis. [2]
items.answer: (a) 6.2 (b) 1000 % (c) Rate increases with light intensity, steeply at low intensities, then levels off at high intensities.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 10⁴/40² = 6.2 (A1). (b) [2] (33 − 3)/3 × 100 (M1) = 1000 % (A1). (c) [2] Positive relationship (A1); levelling off (A1).

items.stem: Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration and explain the role of ATP in cells.
items.answer: ATP structure and hydrolysis; uses: active transport, synthesis, movement; aerobic: O₂, mitochondria, CO₂ + H₂O, ~30 ATP; anaerobic: cytoplasm, lactate or ethanol + CO₂, 2 ATP, NAD regeneration; respirometers; RQ.
items.markingKey: ATP structure and hydrolysis; uses: active transport, synthesis, movement; aerobic: O₂, mitochondria, CO₂ + H₂O, ~30 ATP; anaerobic: cytoplasm, lactate or ethanol + CO₂, 2 ATP, NAD regeneration; respirometers; RQ.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Respiration using oxygen, in which glucose is fully oxidised to CO₂ and water with a large yield of ATP"?
items.answer: aerobic respiration
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of aerobic respiration.

items.stem: Explain why lactate is produced in human muscle during vigorous exercise.
items.answer: Oxygen supply cannot meet demand, so oxidative phosphorylation slows; pyruvate is reduced to lactate using NADH, regenerating NAD so glycolysis can continue to produce a small amount of ATP.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Oxygen supply cannot meet demand, so oxidative phosphorylation slows; pyruvate is reduced to lactate using NADH, regenerating NAD so glycolysis can continue to produce a small amount of ATP. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Yeast in a sealed flask produces CO₂ at a constant rate, but ethanol only appears after several hours. What is the best explanation?
options: Ethanol is made only in light.
Yeast respires aerobically until the oxygen is used up, then switches to anaerobic respiration.
items.answer: Yeast respires aerobically until the oxygen is used up, then switches to anaerobic respiration.
items.markingKey: D. Facultative anaerobe.

items.stem: How many molecules of CO₂ are released per glucose in the link reaction and Krebs cycle combined?
items.markingKey: A. 2 in link reaction + 4 in Krebs cycle.

items.stem: Why does the inner mitochondrial membrane have many folds (cristae)?
options: To allow free diffusion of protons.
To give a large surface area for electron transport chains and ATP synthase.
items.answer: To give a large surface area for electron transport chains and ATP synthase.
items.markingKey: D. Structure–function.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain the link reaction and the Krebs cycle.
items.answer: Pyruvate enters the matrix and is decarboxylated and oxidised, forming acetyl-CoA, CO₂ and NADH; acetyl (2C) combines with oxaloacetate (4C) to form citrate (6C); two decarboxylations and four oxidations regenerate oxaloacetate, releasing 2 CO₂, 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂ and 1 ATP per turn. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Pyruvate enters the matrix and is decarboxylated and oxidised, forming acetyl-CoA, CO₂ and NADH; acetyl (2C) combines with oxaloacetate (4C) to form citrate (6C); two decarboxylations and four oxidations regenerate oxaloacetate, releasing 2 CO₂, 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂ and 1 ATP per turn. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Dinitrophenol makes the inner mitochondrial membrane leaky to protons. Patients taking it lost weight and overheated. Why?
options: Energy from the proton gradient was released as heat instead of making ATP, so more substrate was respired.
items.answer: Energy from the proton gradient was released as heat instead of making ATP, so more substrate was respired.
items.markingKey: B. Uncoupling.

items.stem: How many CO₂ molecules are released per glucose in the link reaction and Krebs cycle combined?
items.markingKey: B. 2 in link reaction, 4 in Krebs.

items.stem: Amara writes: "Most ATP in aerobic respiration is made in the Krebs cycle." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Most ATP is made by oxidative phosphorylation (chemiosmosis); the Krebs cycle makes only 2 ATP per glucose directly.
items.markingKey: Most ATP is made by oxidative phosphorylation (chemiosmosis); the Krebs cycle makes only 2 ATP per glucose directly. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The theoretical yield of 38 ATP per glucose is an accurate description of aerobic respiration."
items.answer: The 38 figure is a theoretical maximum; measured yields are closer to 30, showing the difference between idealised models and real systems.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: counting NADH × 3 and FADH₂ × 2 gives 38 ATP per glucose; it gives a useful comparison with anaerobic respiration. Arguments against: proton leak and transport costs mean the real yield is about 30–32 ATP; the yield varies with the shuttle used to bring NADH into mitochondria. Supported judgement: The 38 figure is a theoretical maximum; measured yields are closer to 30, showing the difference between idealised models and real systems.

items.stem: Describe the stages of aerobic respiration in a eukaryotic cell, including where each occurs and what is produced.
items.answer: Glycolysis (cytoplasm): phosphorylation, lysis, oxidation, 2 pyruvate, net 2 ATP, 2 NADH. Link (matrix): decarboxylation, oxidation, acetyl-CoA, CO₂, NADH. Krebs (matrix): citrate, 2 CO₂, 3 NADH, FADH₂, ATP per turn. ETC (cristae): electrons, proton pumping, gradient, ATP synthase, O₂ final acceptor, water; ~30 ATP.
items.markingKey: Glycolysis (cytoplasm): phosphorylation, lysis, oxidation, 2 pyruvate, net 2 ATP, 2 NADH. Link (matrix): decarboxylation, oxidation, acetyl-CoA, CO₂, NADH. Krebs (matrix): citrate, 2 CO₂, 3 NADH, FADH₂, ATP per turn. ETC (cristae): electrons, proton pumping, gradient, ATP synthase, O₂ final acceptor, water; ~30 ATP.

items.stem: Why does glycolysis require an input of 2 ATP?
options: To make pyruvate leave the cell.
To phosphorylate glucose, making it more reactive (lowering activation energy for lysis).
items.answer: To phosphorylate glucose, making it more reactive (lowering activation energy for lysis).
items.markingKey: C. Phosphorylation before lysis.

items.stem: Explain the difference between substrate-level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation.
items.answer: In substrate-level phosphorylation a phosphate group is transferred directly from a substrate to ADP (glycolysis, Krebs); in oxidative phosphorylation ATP is made by ATP synthase using a proton gradient generated by the electron transport chain.
items.markingKey: In substrate-level phosphorylation a phosphate group is transferred directly from a substrate to ADP (glycolysis, Krebs); in oxidative phosphorylation ATP is made by ATP synthase using a proton gradient generated by the electron transport chain. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to cyanide poisoning, explain how it illustrates the role of oxygen in oxidative phosphorylation.
items.answer: Cyanide binds to cytochrome c oxidase, the final complex of the electron transport chain. Electrons cannot pass to oxygen, so the ETC and chemiosmosis stop and ATP production collapses.
items.markingKey: Context (Cyanide binds to cytochrome c oxidase, the final complex of the electron transport chain.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Electrons cannot pass to oxygen, so the ETC and chemiosmosis stop and ATP production collapses. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the role of oxygen in oxidative phosphorylation.

items.stem:
Pondweed (Elodea) was placed in 1 % sodium hydrogencarbonate solution at 25 °C. A lamp was placed at different distances and the number of bubbles released per minute was counted.

Distance / cm | Relative light intensity (1/d² × 10⁴) | Bubbles per minute
10 | 100.0 | 30
15 | ? | 21
20 | 25.0 | 15
30 | 11.1 | 8
40 | 6.2 | 5
50 | 4.0 | 3

(a) Calculate the relative light intensity at 15 cm. [1]
(b) Calculate the percentage increase in bubble rate from 50 cm to 10 cm. [2]
(c) Describe the relationship between light intensity and the rate of photosynthesis. [2]
(d) Explain why the rate levels off at high light intensity. [2]
(e) Explain why sodium hydrogencarbonate solution was used. [1]
(f) Suggest two limitations of counting bubbles to measure the rate. [2]
(g) Suggest how the effect of the lamp’s heat could be prevented from affecting results. [1]
(h) Suggest how the investigation could be modified to show that CO₂ concentration can become limiting. [2]
items.answer: (a) 44.4 (b) 900 % (c) Rate increases with light intensity, steeply at low intensities, then levels off at high intensities. (d) Another factor, such as CO₂ concentration or temperature, becomes limiting. (e) It provides a supply of CO₂ (as hydrogencarbonate ions) so CO₂ is not limiting at low light. (f) Bubbles vary in size; some O₂ dissolves; bubbles may contain other gases; counting errors at high rates. (g) Place a heat filter / beaker of water between lamp and plant, use an LED, or monitor temperature with a thermometer. (h) Repeat at the highest light intensity with different NaHCO₃ concentrations, keeping temperature constant; the rate should increase with CO₂ concentration.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 10⁴/15² = 44.4 (A1). (b) [2] (30 − 3)/3 × 100 (M1) = 900 % (A1). (c) [2] Positive relationship (A1); levelling off (A1). (d) [2] Another limiting factor named (A1); light no longer limiting (R1). (e) [1] Source of CO₂ (A1). (f) [2] Two valid limitations (A1 A1). (g) [1] Valid method (A1). (h) [2] Vary NaHCO₃ at high light (A1); control of temperature/expected result (A1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "In chromatography, the distance moved by a pigment divided by the distance moved by the solvent front"?
items.answer: Rf value
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of Rf value.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an absorption spectrum and an action spectrum.
items.answer: An absorption spectrum shows how much light each pigment absorbs at each wavelength; an action spectrum shows the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength.
items.markingKey: An absorption spectrum shows how much light each pigment absorbs at each wavelength; an action spectrum shows the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why does the action spectrum closely match the absorption spectrum of chlorophyll?
options: Wavelengths absorbed by pigments are the ones used to drive photosynthesis.
items.answer: Wavelengths absorbed by pigments are the ones used to drive photosynthesis.
items.markingKey: B. Absorbed light used.

items.stem: A student claims: "Plants use green light most because they are green." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Leaves look green because green light is reflected and transmitted; it is absorbed least and so is used least.
items.markingKey: Leaves look green because green light is reflected and transmitted; it is absorbed least and so is used least. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A pigment has an Rf of 0.95 in a non-polar solvent. Which is it most likely to be?
items.answer: carotene
items.markingKey: B. Most soluble, moves furthest.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "LED lighting in vertical farms should provide only red and blue light."
items.answer: Red and blue give the most photosynthesis per unit energy, but adding some green and far-red improves growth and canopy photosynthesis.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: red and blue are absorbed most and drive photosynthesis efficiently, saving energy; growers report good yields with red/blue LEDs. Arguments against: some green light penetrates deeper into the canopy and drives photosynthesis in lower leaves; other wavelengths affect plant development and allow workers to see plant health. Supported judgement: Red and blue give the most photosynthesis per unit energy, but adding some green and far-red improves growth and canopy photosynthesis.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "absorption spectrum".
items.answer: A graph showing the percentage of light absorbed by a pigment at each wavelength
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a graph showing the percentage of light absorbed by a pigment at each wavelength. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: In a chromatogram of a leaf extract the solvent front moved 7.5 cm. The spots moved: spot 1 (orange-yellow) 7.1 cm; spot 2 (grey) 6.2 cm. Calculate the Rf value of each spot and identify the pigments, using reference values carotene 0.95, phaeophytin 0.83, xanthophyll 0.71, chlorophyll a 0.60, chlorophyll b 0.47.
items.answer: spot 1: Rf 0.95 = carotene; spot 2: Rf 0.83 = phaeophytin
items.markingKey: Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent (M1); 7.1/7.5 = 0.95 → carotene; 6.2/7.5 = 0.83 → phaeophytin (A1 each).

items.stem: Describe how photosynthetic pigments can be separated by chromatography and explain the relationship between absorption and action spectra.
items.answer: Extract in solvent; spot; develop; solvent front; Rf; identify carotene, xanthophyll, chlorophyll a, b; absorption spectra of pigments; action spectrum peaks red/blue; trough green; accessory pigments widen range; Engelmann.
items.markingKey: Extract in solvent; spot; develop; solvent front; Rf; identify carotene, xanthophyll, chlorophyll a, b; absorption spectra of pigments; action spectrum peaks red/blue; trough green; accessory pigments widen range; Engelmann.

items.stem: What is the source of the oxygen released in photosynthesis?
items.answer: water, split by photolysis
items.markingKey: water, split by photolysis. Shown with ¹⁸O isotopes.

items.stem: Why does the Calvin cycle stop in the dark?
options: ATP and reduced NADP from the light-dependent reactions are no longer supplied.
items.answer: ATP and reduced NADP from the light-dependent reactions are no longer supplied.
items.markingKey: C. Dependence on products.

items.stem: Explain the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis.
items.answer: Light absorbed by photosystem II excites electrons, which pass along an electron transport chain to photosystem I; energy is used to pump protons into the thylakoid lumen; photolysis of water replaces electrons and releases O₂ and H⁺; protons diffuse through ATP synthase making ATP; PSI re-excites electrons, which reduce NADP.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Light absorbed by photosystem II excites electrons, which pass along an electron transport chain to photosystem I; energy is used to pump protons into the thylakoid lumen; photolysis of water replaces electrons and releases O₂ and H⁺; protons diffuse through ATP synthase making ATP; PSI re-excites electrons, which reduce NADP. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Calculate the number of CO₂ molecules fixed, turns of the Calvin cycle and molecules of ATP and NADPH used to produce 2 glucose molecules.
items.answer: 12 CO₂; 12 turns; 36 ATP; 24 NADPH
items.markingKey: 6 CO₂ and 6 turns per glucose (A1); 18 ATP and 12 NADPH per glucose (A1); × 2 (A1).

items.stem: In Calvin’s “lollipop” experiment, ¹⁴C appeared first in which compound after 5 seconds?
items.answer: glycerate 3-phosphate
items.markingKey: A. The first stable product of fixation.

items.stem: Using Melvin Calvin’s “lollipop” apparatus experiments (1950s) as an example, explain the light-independent reactions.
items.answer: Chlorella was given ¹⁴CO₂ for seconds, then killed in hot methanol; compounds were separated by chromatography. Labelled carbon appeared first in GP, then triose phosphate and RuBP, revealing the order of reactions in the cycle.
items.markingKey: Context (Chlorella was given ¹⁴CO₂ for seconds, then killed in hot methanol; compounds were separated by chromatography.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Labelled carbon appeared first in GP, then triose phosphate and RuBP, revealing the order of reactions in the cycle. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the light-independent reactions.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Improving RuBisCO is the best way to increase crop yields."
items.answer: RuBisCO is a major bottleneck, but yield depends on many factors; improving it is one promising approach among several.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: RuBisCO is slow and also reacts with oxygen (photorespiration), wasting energy; engineering faster or more CO₂-specific RuBisCO could raise efficiency. Arguments against: yields are often limited by water, nutrients or light capture instead; RuBisCO is hard to engineer without losing specificity; other approaches (C4 rice, better canopy) may be easier. Supported judgement: RuBisCO is a major bottleneck, but yield depends on many factors; improving it is one promising approach among several.

items.stem: Explain how light energy is converted into chemical energy in the chloroplast.
items.answer: Photosystems absorb light; excited electrons; ETC; proton pumping into lumen; photolysis O₂; ATP synthase chemiosmosis; NADP reduced; Calvin cycle: RuBisCO fixes CO₂ to RuBP, GP reduced to TP with ATP/NADPH; RuBP regenerated; glucose/starch; locations.
items.markingKey: Photosystems absorb light; excited electrons; ETC; proton pumping into lumen; photolysis O₂; ATP synthase chemiosmosis; NADP reduced; Calvin cycle: RuBisCO fixes CO₂ to RuBP, GP reduced to TP with ATP/NADPH; RuBP regenerated; glucose/starch; locations.

items.stem: Why does the Calvin cycle stop shortly after a plant is put in darkness?
options: ATP and NADPH from the light-dependent reactions run out.
CO₂ is not available in darkness.
RuBisCO is denatured in the dark.
items.answer: ATP and NADPH from the light-dependent reactions run out.
items.markingKey: A. The cycle depends on light reactions.

items.stem: Distinguish between non-cyclic photophosphorylation and cyclic photophosphorylation.
items.answer: In cyclic photophosphorylation electrons from PSI return to the ETC, producing ATP only; in non-cyclic, electrons flow from water through PSII and PSI to NADP, producing ATP, NADPH and O₂.
items.markingKey: In cyclic photophosphorylation electrons from PSI return to the ETC, producing ATP only; in non-cyclic, electrons flow from water through PSII and PSI to NADP, producing ATP, NADPH and O₂. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: If CO₂ is suddenly reduced, what happens to RuBP and GP?
items.answer: RuBP rises and GP falls.
items.markingKey: C. Less carboxylation.

items.stem: Which method measures the rate of photosynthesis of pondweed?
items.answer: counting bubbles or collecting O₂ released per minute
items.markingKey: counting bubbles or collecting O₂ released per minute. O₂ production indicates rate.

items.stem: "Doubling the distance of a lamp halves the light intensity." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of distance, so doubling distance reduces intensity to a quarter.
items.markingKey: Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of distance, so doubling distance reduces intensity to a quarter. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Why can increasing temperature raise the rate of photosynthesis only up to a point?
options: CO₂ cannot dissolve at high temperatures.
Enzymes such as RuBisCO work faster until they begin to denature above the optimum.
Light reactions stop at low temperature.
items.answer: Enzymes such as RuBisCO work faster until they begin to denature above the optimum.
items.markingKey: C. Enzyme-controlled.

items.stem: Outline one way in which tomato growers in the Netherlands using CO₂ enrichment shows carbon dioxide as a limiting factor.
items.answer: Greenhouses are enriched to about 800–1000 ppm CO₂ using waste CO₂ from industry or heaters. In bright, warm conditions CO₂ limits photosynthesis, so raising it increases yields.
items.markingKey: Context (Greenhouses are enriched to about 800–1000 ppm CO₂ using waste CO₂ from industry or heaters.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: In bright, warm conditions CO₂ limits photosynthesis, so raising it increases yields. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to carbon dioxide as a limiting factor.

items.stem: The rate of oxygen production by an alga changed from 58.0 to 42.1 µmol h⁻¹ when the temperature was raised from 25 °C to 40 °C. Calculate the percentage change and suggest a biological explanation for it.
items.answer: -27.4 %; above the optimum, enzymes of the Calvin cycle denature and photorespiration rises.
items.markingKey: % change = (42.1 − 58.0)/58.0 × 100 (M1) = -27.4 % (A1). Explanation (R1): above the optimum, enzymes of the Calvin cycle denature and photorespiration rises.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Rising atmospheric CO₂ will greatly increase global crop yields."
items.answer: CO₂ fertilisation gives modest gains that are likely to be outweighed by the negative effects of climate change, so large yield increases are unlikely.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: CO₂ is often limiting, and FACE trials show some yield increase in C3 crops; higher CO₂ improves water-use efficiency as stomata close partially. Arguments against: FACE increases are smaller than expected and lower the protein and mineral content of grain; higher temperatures, droughts and floods linked to climate change will reduce yields. Supported judgement: CO₂ fertilisation gives modest gains that are likely to be outweighed by the negative effects of climate change, so large yield increases are unlikely.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "free-air carbon dioxide enrichment (FACE)".
items.answer: Field experiments in which CO₂ is released around plants in the open to study the effects of future CO₂ levels
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: field experiments in which CO₂ is released around plants in the open to study the effects of future CO₂ levels. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: At the light compensation point, what is the net gas exchange of a leaf?
items.answer: zero – photosynthesis equals respiration
items.markingKey: D. Balance.

items.stem: Explain how light intensity, CO₂ concentration and temperature limit the rate of photosynthesis, and evaluate the use of CO₂ enrichment in greenhouses.
items.answer: Limiting factor concept; graphs and plateaus; light → light-dependent reactions; CO₂ → RuBisCO fixation; temperature → enzymes, denaturation; inverse square law; greenhouses: CO₂ 1000 ppm, cost vs yield, heating, lighting; FACE results; other limits.
items.markingKey: Limiting factor concept; graphs and plateaus; light → light-dependent reactions; CO₂ → RuBisCO fixation; temperature → enzymes, denaturation; inverse square law; greenhouses: CO₂ 1000 ppm, cost vs yield, heating, lighting; FACE results; other limits.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A cycle of reactions in the mitochondrial matrix in which acetyl groups are oxidised, releasing CO₂ and producing reduced NAD, reduced FAD and ATP"?
items.answer: Krebs cycle
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of Krebs cycle.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Calvin cycle"?
options: Apparatus used to measure the rate of oxygen uptake by respiring organisms
Adenosine triphosphate, a nucleotide that acts as the immediately available energy currency of the cell
The light-independent reactions in the stroma in which CO₂ is fixed by RuBisCO and reduced to triose phosphate using ATP and NADPH
The value of a factor above which further increases do not increase the rate of photosynthesis because another factor is limiting
items.answer: The light-independent reactions in the stroma in which CO₂ is fixed by RuBisCO and reduced to triose phosphate using ATP and NADPH
items.markingKey: C. "Calvin cycle" is the light-independent reactions in the stroma in which CO₂ is fixed by RuBisCO and reduced to triose phosphate using ATP and NADPH.

items.stem: Approximately how much ATP does aerobic respiration yield per glucose compared with anaerobic?
items.answer: about 30 molecules compared with 2
items.markingKey: about 30 molecules compared with 2. Oxidative phosphorylation produces most ATP.

items.stem: Why does a mixture of pigments benefit a plant?
options: Different pigments absorb different wavelengths, widening the range of light used.
All pigments absorb the same wavelengths.
items.answer: Different pigments absorb different wavelengths, widening the range of light used.
items.markingKey: A. Accessory pigments extend absorption.

items.stem: Explain the concept of limiting factors in photosynthesis.
items.answer: The rate of photosynthesis is limited by whichever factor is in shortest supply (light, CO₂ or temperature); increasing that factor increases the rate until another becomes limiting, giving a plateau; only increasing the new limiting factor raises the rate further.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The rate of photosynthesis is limited by whichever factor is in shortest supply (light, CO₂ or temperature); increasing that factor increases the rate until another becomes limiting, giving a plateau; only increasing the new limiting factor raises the rate further. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between oxidative phosphorylation and substrate-level phosphorylation.
items.answer: In substrate-level phosphorylation a phosphate group is transferred directly from a substrate to ADP (glycolysis, Krebs); in oxidative phosphorylation ATP is made by ATP synthase using a proton gradient generated by the electron transport chain.
items.markingKey: In substrate-level phosphorylation a phosphate group is transferred directly from a substrate to ADP (glycolysis, Krebs); in oxidative phosphorylation ATP is made by ATP synthase using a proton gradient generated by the electron transport chain. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Amara writes: "The light-independent reactions happen only at night." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: They occur in the light (they need ATP and NADPH from the light-dependent reactions); they are “light-independent” because they do not use light directly.
items.markingKey: They occur in the light (they need ATP and NADPH from the light-dependent reactions); they are “light-independent” because they do not use light directly. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "ATP is a long-term energy store." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: ATP is an immediate energy source; long-term energy is stored as fats and glycogen/starch.
items.markingKey: ATP is an immediate energy source; long-term energy is stored as fats and glycogen/starch. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why the action spectrum of photosynthesis has peaks in the blue and red regions.
items.answer: Chlorophyll a and b absorb blue (about 430–450 nm) and red (about 640–680 nm) light strongly; absorbed light energy excites electrons in the photosystems, driving the light-dependent reactions, so these wavelengths give the highest rates.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Chlorophyll a and b absorb blue (about 430–450 nm) and red (about 640–680 nm) light strongly; absorbed light energy excites electrons in the photosystems, driving the light-dependent reactions, so these wavelengths give the highest rates. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A lamp is moved from 20 cm to 10 cm from pondweed. By what factor does light intensity increase?
items.markingKey: D. Light intensity ∝ 1/d²: (20/10)² = 4.

items.stem: Calculate the number of turns of the Krebs cycle when 4 molecules of glucose are respired aerobically.
items.markingKey: 2 acetyl-CoA per glucose × 4 = 8 (A1).

items.stem: Calculate the number of CO₂ molecules fixed, turns of the Calvin cycle and molecules of ATP and NADPH used to produce 5 glucose molecules.
items.answer: 30 CO₂; 30 turns; 90 ATP; 60 NADPH
items.markingKey: 6 CO₂ and 6 turns per glucose (A1); 18 ATP and 12 NADPH per glucose (A1); × 5 (A1).

items.stem: During a sprint, lactate concentration in muscle rises. Why?
options: Lactate is a product of the Krebs cycle.
Oxygen supply is insufficient, so pyruvate is reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD.
items.answer: Oxygen supply is insufficient, so pyruvate is reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD.
items.markingKey: C. Anaerobic respiration.

items.stem: Elodea in green light produces few bubbles, but many in red and blue light. What does this show?
options: Elodea does not photosynthesise in red light.
The rate of photosynthesis depends on the wavelengths absorbed by chlorophyll.
items.answer: The rate of photosynthesis depends on the wavelengths absorbed by chlorophyll.
items.markingKey: D. Matches absorption spectrum.

items.stem: Kwame writes: "Plants photosynthesise faster the hotter it gets." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Above the optimum temperature enzymes such as RuBisCO denature and photorespiration increases, so the rate falls.
items.markingKey: Above the optimum temperature enzymes such as RuBisCO denature and photorespiration increases, so the rate falls. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Protons are pumped into the matrix by the electron transport chain." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Protons are pumped from the matrix into the intermembrane space; they flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase.
items.markingKey: Protons are pumped from the matrix into the intermembrane space; they flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

Distance / cm | Relative light intensity (1/d² × 10⁴) | Bubbles per minute

items.stem: "Anaerobic respiration is an inefficient process that is of little value to organisms." Discuss.
items.answer: It is inefficient in ATP per glucose, but very valuable as a rapid, oxygen-independent source of ATP.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it yields only 2 ATP per glucose compared with about 30; lactate accumulation causes fatigue. Arguments against: it allows ATP production when oxygen is limited, e.g. in sprints or waterlogged roots; yeast fermentation is the basis of brewing and baking. Supported judgement: It is inefficient in ATP per glucose, but very valuable as a rapid, oxygen-independent source of ATP. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: "LED lighting in vertical farms should provide only red and blue light." Discuss.
items.answer: Red and blue give the most photosynthesis per unit energy, but adding some green and far-red improves growth and canopy photosynthesis.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: red and blue are absorbed most and drive photosynthesis efficiently, saving energy; growers report good yields with red/blue LEDs. Arguments against: some green light penetrates deeper into the canopy and drives photosynthesis in lower leaves; other wavelengths affect plant development and allow workers to see plant health. Supported judgement: Red and blue give the most photosynthesis per unit energy, but adding some green and far-red improves growth and canopy photosynthesis. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: "Rising atmospheric CO₂ will greatly increase global crop yields." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: CO₂ fertilisation gives modest gains that are likely to be outweighed by the negative effects of climate change, so large yield increases are unlikely.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: CO₂ is often limiting, and FACE trials show some yield increase in C3 crops; higher CO₂ improves water-use efficiency as stomata close partially. Arguments against: FACE increases are smaller than expected and lower the protein and mineral content of grain; higher temperatures, droughts and floods linked to climate change will reduce yields. Supported judgement: CO₂ fertilisation gives modest gains that are likely to be outweighed by the negative effects of climate change, so large yield increases are unlikely. Markbands (8 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "link reaction".
items.answer: The oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate in the mitochondrial matrix to form acetyl-CoA, releasing CO₂ and reducing NAD
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate in the mitochondrial matrix to form acetyl-CoA, releasing CO₂ and reducing NAD. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Where do the light-dependent reactions take place?
items.answer: in the thylakoid membranes
items.markingKey: D. Photosystems and ATP synthase are in thylakoids.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "anaerobic respiration"?
options: The loss of electrons or hydrogen (or gain of oxygen) by a substance
Respiration without oxygen, which yields a small amount of ATP; lactate in animals, ethanol and CO₂ in yeast and plants
The removal of carbon as CO₂ from a molecule
A molecule that absorbs specific wavelengths of light for photosynthesis, such as chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b and carotenoids
items.answer: Respiration without oxygen, which yields a small amount of ATP; lactate in animals, ethanol and CO₂ in yeast and plants
items.markingKey: B. "anaerobic respiration" is respiration without oxygen, which yields a small amount of ATP; lactate in animals, ethanol and CO₂ in yeast and plants.

items.stem: Distinguish between carotenoids and chlorophyll a.
items.answer: Chlorophyll a is the primary pigment at reaction centres, absorbing red and blue light and appearing blue-green; carotenoids are accessory pigments that absorb blue–green light, appear yellow-orange and protect chlorophyll from excess light.
items.markingKey: Chlorophyll a is the primary pigment at reaction centres, absorbing red and blue light and appearing blue-green; carotenoids are accessory pigments that absorb blue–green light, appear yellow-orange and protect chlorophyll from excess light. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a CO₂-limited rate and a light-limited rate.
items.answer: When light is limiting, increasing light raises the rate while increasing CO₂ has little effect; when CO₂ is limiting, increasing CO₂ raises the rate while extra light has little effect.
items.markingKey: When light is limiting, increasing light raises the rate while increasing CO₂ has little effect; when CO₂ is limiting, increasing CO₂ raises the rate while extra light has little effect. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: How do electrons in the ETC generate a proton gradient?
options: Energy released as electrons pass between carriers is used to pump protons into the intermembrane space.
Electrons carry protons through ATP synthase.
ATP pumps protons out of the matrix.
items.answer: Energy released as electrons pass between carriers is used to pump protons into the intermembrane space.
items.markingKey: B. Proton pumping by complexes.

items.stem: Distinguish between cyclic photophosphorylation and non-cyclic photophosphorylation.
items.answer: In cyclic photophosphorylation electrons from PSI return to the ETC, producing ATP only; in non-cyclic, electrons flow from water through PSII and PSI to NADP, producing ATP, NADPH and O₂.
items.markingKey: In cyclic photophosphorylation electrons from PSI return to the ETC, producing ATP only; in non-cyclic, electrons flow from water through PSII and PSI to NADP, producing ATP, NADPH and O₂. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between anaerobic respiration in humans and anaerobic respiration in yeast.
items.answer: Yeast converts pyruvate to ethanol and CO₂; humans convert pyruvate to lactate with no CO₂ released; both regenerate NAD and yield 2 ATP per glucose.
items.markingKey: Yeast converts pyruvate to ethanol and CO₂; humans convert pyruvate to lactate with no CO₂ released; both regenerate NAD and yield 2 ATP per glucose. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how chromatography can be used to separate and identify photosynthetic pigments.
items.answer: Pigment extract is spotted on a baseline; the strip is placed in solvent below the line; solvent moves up carrying pigments at different rates depending on solubility and adsorption; Rf values (distance pigment/distance solvent) and colours are compared with known values to identify them.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Pigment extract is spotted on a baseline; the strip is placed in solvent below the line; solvent moves up carrying pigments at different rates depending on solubility and adsorption; Rf values (distance pigment/distance solvent) and colours are compared with known values to identify them. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe tomato growers in the Netherlands using CO₂ enrichment and explain what it reveals about carbon dioxide as a limiting factor.
items.answer: Greenhouses are enriched to about 800–1000 ppm CO₂ using waste CO₂ from industry or heaters. In bright, warm conditions CO₂ limits photosynthesis, so raising it increases yields.
items.markingKey: Context (Greenhouses are enriched to about 800–1000 ppm CO₂ using waste CO₂ from industry or heaters.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: In bright, warm conditions CO₂ limits photosynthesis, so raising it increases yields. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to carbon dioxide as a limiting factor.

items.stem: Calculate the number of molecules of ATP produced by substrate-level phosphorylation (net) when 2 molecules of glucose are respired aerobically.
items.markingKey: net 2 (glycolysis) + 2 (Krebs) = 4 per glucose × 2 = 8 (A1).

items.stem: With reference to Ruben and Kamen’s experiments with ¹⁸O (1941), explain how it illustrates photolysis.
items.answer: When water contained ¹⁸O, the oxygen released was labelled; when CO₂ was labelled it was not. Isotope labelling showed the oxygen released comes from water.
items.markingKey: Context (When water contained ¹⁸O, the oxygen released was labelled; when CO₂ was labelled it was not.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Isotope labelling showed the oxygen released comes from water. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to photolysis.

items.stem: With reference to sprint training and lactate threshold in athletes, explain how it illustrates anaerobic respiration in humans.
items.answer: During a 400 m sprint blood lactate can rise more than tenfold. When oxygen supply is insufficient, muscles regenerate NAD by making lactate, allowing a short burst of ATP production.
items.markingKey: Context (During a 400 m sprint blood lactate can rise more than tenfold.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: When oxygen supply is insufficient, muscles regenerate NAD by making lactate, allowing a short burst of ATP production. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to anaerobic respiration in humans.

items.stem: With reference to autumn colour change in deciduous trees such as maples, explain how it illustrates the presence of several photosynthetic pigments.
items.answer: Chlorophyll is broken down before leaf fall, revealing yellow-orange carotenoids. Carotenoids were present all along as accessory pigments, masked by chlorophyll.
items.markingKey: Context (Chlorophyll is broken down before leaf fall, revealing yellow-orange carotenoids.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Carotenoids were present all along as accessory pigments, masked by chlorophyll. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the presence of several photosynthetic pigments.

items.stem: Paraffin heaters are used in a greenhouse. Which two limiting factors are increased?
items.answer: temperature and CO₂ concentration
items.markingKey: D. Combustion.

items.markingKey: B. 2 (link) + 6 (Krebs).

items.stem:
Pondweed (Elodea) was placed in 1 % sodium hydrogencarbonate solution at 25 °C. A lamp was placed at different distances and the number of bubbles released per minute was counted.

Distance / cm | Relative light intensity (1/d² × 10⁴) | Bubbles per minute
10 | 100.0 | 28
15 | 44.4 | 19
20 | 25.0 | 13
30 | 11.1 | 7
40 | ? | 4
50 | 4.0 | 3

(a) Calculate the relative light intensity at 40 cm. [1]
(b) Calculate the percentage increase in bubble rate from 50 cm to 10 cm. [2]
(c) Describe the relationship between light intensity and the rate of photosynthesis. [2]
(d) Explain why the rate levels off at high light intensity. [2]
(e) Explain why sodium hydrogencarbonate solution was used. [1]
(f) Suggest two limitations of counting bubbles to measure the rate. [2]
(g) Suggest how the effect of the lamp’s heat could be prevented from affecting results. [1]
(h) Suggest how the investigation could be modified to show that CO₂ concentration can become limiting. [2]
items.answer: (a) 6.2 (b) 833 % (c) Rate increases with light intensity, steeply at low intensities, then levels off at high intensities. (d) Another factor, such as CO₂ concentration or temperature, becomes limiting. (e) It provides a supply of CO₂ (as hydrogencarbonate ions) so CO₂ is not limiting at low light. (f) Bubbles vary in size; some O₂ dissolves; bubbles may contain other gases; counting errors at high rates. (g) Place a heat filter / beaker of water between lamp and plant, use an LED, or monitor temperature with a thermometer. (h) Repeat at the highest light intensity with different NaHCO₃ concentrations, keeping temperature constant; the rate should increase with CO₂ concentration.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 10⁴/40² = 6.2 (A1). (b) [2] (28 − 3)/3 × 100 (M1) = 833 % (A1). (c) [2] Positive relationship (A1); levelling off (A1). (d) [2] Another limiting factor named (A1); light no longer limiting (R1). (e) [1] Source of CO₂ (A1). (f) [2] Two valid limitations (A1 A1). (g) [1] Valid method (A1). (h) [2] Vary NaHCO₃ at high light (A1); control of temperature/expected result (A1).
